problem: Prior hand-drawn-map robot navigation (heuristic and probabilistic methods) needs metrically accurate sketches, hand-crafted simple landmarks and a single floor, and cannot cope with missing or misplaced landmarks. VLN methods require complete verbal instructions in one utterance.
motivation: Hand-drawn maps are a natural, cheap way for humans to convey routes without prior map acquisition or exploration. Sketches made from memory are distorted and incomplete, so a method must be robust to scale errors, missing landmarks and multi-floor layouts. Pre-trained VLMs offer common-sense reasoning and visual-text grounding that can fill these gaps zero-shot.
key_idea: Overlay a dynamically pruned topological map on the hand-drawn map next to the robot's current view (Selective Visual Association Prompting) so a VLM can localize and choose actions zero-shot, while a Predictive Navigation Plan Parser uses VLM common sense to infer omitted landmarks.
insight: The ablations show every component matters, with the experience memory being most critical: removing EM drops SR from 80% to 5%, removing the pruned topological map drops it to 25%, and removing predicted landmarks to 40%. Performance also depends heavily on VLM strength: Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B/72B reach 28/38/65% SR versus 80% for GPT-4o. Structured visual prompts plus history and landmark priors compensate for sketch inaccuracies.
method: Topological Map Generator (TMG): builds a graph of robot-position nodes and landmark nodes (via OCR) from the hand-drawn map, and is updated with VLM-predicted landmarks.

Spatial Interpreter (SI): detects object landmarks with Grounding DINO and structural landmarks (left/right turns) via Grounded-SAM traversable mask, Hough edges and rules; also builds a scene description with left/front/right landmark positions passed to the VLM.
Experience Manager (EM): stores past (scene description, position, action) tuples and retrieves the most similar via cosine similarity (RAG) as textual context.

Visual Prompt Generator (VPG): builds the SVAP image, with the robot view next to the hand-drawn map overlaid with a topological map pruned by a logistic retention probability (nodes kept if >0.5; β=2, α=γ=0.5).
Predictive Navigation Plan Parser (PNPP): the VLM infers co-occurring missing landmarks per node and segments the route at junctions into a textual navigation plan.
Localization Engine and Navigation Planning Engine: a VLM with CoT and score-based prompting selects the position node, then a discrete action (forward/left/right/stop).
Navigation Controller: projects the traversable-mask centroid or the turn-junction pixel to a 3D goal via a pinhole model, then uses a global planner (A*/RRT) and local planner (TEB/NMPC).

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) plus Grounding DINO and Grounded-SAM; Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B/72B as ablation backbones
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D camera plus the hand-drawn map
setting.action_space: discrete high-level actions (move forward, turn left, turn right, stop) converted to velocities via a planner
setting.privileged: none (the human hand-drawn map with the path is the input)

numbers_note: No standard VLN benchmarks; results are on custom Gazebo environments and a real-world user study. Baselines omitted per rules.
results: In simulation HAM-Nav (GPT-4o) reaches 80% SR and 0.712 SPL, far above every ablation, with the best open-source Qwen2.5-72B at 65% SR. In the real-world user study it beats the VLN method MapGPT on all metrics (SR 77% vs 64%, SPL 0.703 vs 0.523) and on usability (SUS 79.5 vs 47.25).
limitations: Long navigation time from stop-and-go behavior while waiting for VLM API outputs, and it requires internet access.
Common failure is incorrect localization leading to loops or dead ends, especially with sparse maps lacking landmark labels.
Evaluation is limited to custom small-scale environments (2 sim, 3 real) and depends on strong proprietary GPT-4o; open-source models perform notably worse.
builds_on: Score-based prompting (Shah et al. LLM semantic guesswork)
